data.title: Rare red carpet in KL for Myanmarâs leader sparks outrage, but signals shifting Asean stance
data.description:
[BANGKOK] Myanmar’s Min Aung Hlaing has wrapped up an official two-day visit to Malaysia – his fifth to a regional country in 2026 – amid outcry against Putrajaya for welcoming him without extracting commitments on ending violence.

During his visit that wrapped up on Thursday (Oct 8), he met Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and both agreed on advancing cooperation in sectors like education, energy and healthcare. However, no pacts were inked.

“I firmly believe that enhancing our bilateral economic cooperation will bring highly practical economic benefits and joint opportunities for the people of both countries,” Min Aung Hlaing said in a joint press conference on Thursday.

“I also wish to invite Malaysian business leaders from various sectors to come and invest in Myanmar, a country that has excellent investment opportunities,” he added.

Since Min Aung Hlaing assumed the presidency in April after a carefully orchestrated election held from December to January 2026, he has visited Asean states Laos, Thailand, Vietnam and Cambodia.

But the visit to Malaysia has raised eyebrows especially given that Putrajaya used to be one of the harshest critics of the coup carried out by the Myanmar military regime in 2021.

Since the February 2021 coup which Min Aung Hlaing staged, Asean has barred him from all leaders’ summits. However, half of the 11-member Asean group have now laid out the red carpet for him, normalising ties with the former junta leader.

Repatriation high on the agenda

In Kuala Lumpur though, the repatriation of Myanmar nationals was high on the agenda with more expected to be sent back.

During the same press conference, Anwar praised Min Aung Hlaing for being “very cooperative” on the matter.

“Many of us do not realise that hardly any country in my experience are willing to accept this repatriation in large numbers at their own expense as you have shown,” Anwar said.

But to Rohingya activist and former Myanmar political prisoner Wai Wai Nu, “the plan is not just morally bankrupt but it makes no practical sense”.

“Deporting refugees to Myanmar under an agreement with Min Aung Hlaing is a violation of international law and against the fundamental principle of non-refoulement,” she said.

Currently, the western Rakhine state where most of the Rohingya refugees are from is largely under the control of ethnic Arakan Army and not the military regime.

“The (repatriation) plan will fail while emboldening Min Aung Hlaing and fuelling instability, making a lasting solution harder to reach,” Wai Wai Nu added.

Matthew Smith, chief executive officer and founder of civil society Fortify Rights, said that welcoming Min Aung Hlaing while returning Myanmar nationals “sends a devastating and wrong message”.

According to the Institute for Strategy and Policy-Myanmar, an independent think-tank based in Thailand, the military conducted at least 1,583 aerial attacks in just five months from Mar 31 to Aug 31 in 2026.

Rights groups chastise the visit

Malaysia’s engagement with Min Aung Hlaing has outraged rights activists, with Charles Santiago, co-chair of Asean Parliamentarians for Human Rights saying the visit “has legitimised” the Myanmar leader’s political status and was “a win” for him.

“Diplomacy is not merely about having a conversation. It is about leverage, accountability, consequences and outcomes. Why should we believe that another bilateral conversation will succeed where years of Asean engagement have failed?” Santiago asked.

Debbie Stothard, founder and coordinator of ALTSEAN-Burma, an advocacy and rights non-government organisation based in Thailand called the visit “a significant sell-out by Malaysia”.

This came after Malaysian Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan told the Parliament on Jun 25 that Kuala Lumpur does not recognise Myanmar’s post-election administration.

“I have already stated that we do not recognise them. When we do not recognise them, the term ‘government’ does not apply from Malaysia’s perspective,” he had insisted.

However, on Thursday, Malaysia’s Anwar changed his tone.

“We, of course, are reminded of the Asean mechanism but we also understand that the President and your government have made a lot of efforts in order to enhance better relations but to have the necessary reform, policy changes, adjustments in your own country,” Anwar said.

“We, on our part in Malaysia, will do whatever is possible to make sure that we enhance this collaboration and ultimately take Myanmar as part of our community of nations without prejudice and particularly in the context of Asean,” he added.

Stothard added that repatriating Myanmar citizens boycotting tax payments to the junta, and replacing them with the regime’s approved batch of documented Myanmar workers to Malaysia, is another way the military-linked government seeks to earn tax revenue.

Focus on repatriation scale

The repatriation of almost 200,000 Myanmar nationals living in Malaysia including Rohingya Muslims, a stateless minority, is a major topic between the two nations.

During the press conference, both leaders said their respective ministries will coordinate the deportation process.

“We will expedite the process to bring them back and we are sending one naval ship to Malaysia for their repatriation,” said Min Aung Hlaing.

The Rohingya have long been discriminated against in Myanmar and a brutal military crackdown in 2017 forced at least 700,000 to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh, where they now live in the world’s largest refugee camp.

Anwar previously said no Rohingya Muslims have been repatriated so far, even as he informed the Malaysian Parliament on Tuesday that more than 10,000 Myanmar nationals have been sent home since January 2026.

And just a week before Min Aung Hlaing’s visit, Malaysia deported almost 2,000 Myanmar nationals on Sep 29.

Analysts said this move serves Anwar’s political survival, as Malaysians’ resentment towards this group swells.

“Anwar’s metric at this stage is how to win Malay votes because he has been losing popularity ahead of Malaysia’s expected general election,” said Stothard.

Meanwhile, Khoo Ying Hooi, an associate professor of international relations and human rights at Universiti Malaya’s Department of International and Strategic Studies, described the deportation as problematic.

Though Myanmar has given the assurance that the returnees will be safe and protected, she said sending them back to a country that is still engaged in active violent conflicts is worrying.

Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, an independent global conflict monitor, reported that since the coup, at least 100,000 people have died. The deportees also risk being subjected to forced conscription by the junta.

Khoo said Malaysia needs to extract more tangible commitments from Myanmar such as allowing independent monitoring and clear procedures for identifying people who require international protection.

“Malaysia could also use the meeting to press for humanitarian access and some demonstrable movement on the broader Asean agenda,” she suggested.

Asean peace plan weakens

Asean maintains its ban on Min Aung Hlaing and expects him to substantially implement the 2021 Five-Point Consensus (5PC), which includes ending violence and allowing greater humanitarian aid delivery access among other conditions before reinstating his participation.

But Min Aung Hlaing has largely disregarded the peace plan, claiming Myanmar’s pro-military parliamentarians have rejected it.

The two leaders made no mention of the 5PC when making statements at the joint press conference.

As recently as Sep 28, the Myanmar military reportedly conducted an air strike on a market in western Rakhine state, killing some 50 civilians.

“When relatively limited concessions receive prominent diplomatic recognition while mass civilian casualties produce a much weaker collective political response, Asean risks appearing to lower its own benchmark for progress,” Khoo said.

“That is particularly problematic because cessation of violence is at the heart of the Five-Point Consensus,” she added.

Independent Myanmar analyst Wai Yan Phyo Naing said the bilateral visits also send a wrong message to the wider global community. He said nations may use political justification as an excuse to restore diplomatic contact without requiring meaningful concessions from the junta.

“Such engagement would further legitimise Min Aung Hlaing, weaken international pressure, and marginalise Myanmar’s democratic forces. It is particularly dangerous because the junta may interpret normalisation as evidence that violence and repression have no serious diplomatic consequences,” said Wai Yan Phyo Naing.

Myanmar, Khoo said, will be a major test for Asean on whether the grouping can distinguish between necessary diplomatic engagement and full political normalisation.

“One visit becomes several visits, and eventually the argument shifts from whether governments should engage Min Aung Hlaing to why they should continue isolating him when his own neighbours no longer do so,” she said. THE STRAITS TIMES

data.title: Airlines are upgrading Wi-Fi. Not all are using Elon Muskâs Starlink
data.description:
IN-FLIGHT Wi-Fi has long been slow and erratic. But airlines are racing to change that.

Hoping that faster, more reliable Internet access will help them attract and retain customers, many carriers are upgrading their planes to use Starlink, the satellite Internet service operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.

On Thursday (Oct 8), American Airlines said that it would outfit more than 1,000 planes with Starlink.

But Delta Air Lines has chosen not to go with the provider, which has upset Musk, SpaceX’s CEO.

Musk said in September that Delta’s CEO would “lose his job” for choosing Amazon’s satellite service; he previously attacked the top executive of Ryanair, a European carrier, for snubbing Starlink, too.

More recently, he said that Indian oligarchs were blocking Starlink there, which he called “a crime against the people of India”.

From fee to free

Lufthansa was the first commercial airline to offer in-flight Internet access in 2004, using a service developed by Boeing. But Boeing shut down the project just two years later.

Other providers filled the void, and US airlines started to offer Wi-Fi in the late 2000s. But few passengers used those services, which were often expensive, slow and unreliable. Over the years, the costs started to fall.

In 2023, Delta eliminated Wi-Fi fees for members of the company’s loyalty programme. JetBlue Airways had been offering free Internet access for years – but Delta kicked off an industry shift.

Why is Wi-Fi so important?

Many airlines offer free Internet service to passengers who sign up for frequent flyer programmes. The programmes allow the companies to collect more information about travellers and to encourage them to buy more tickets and sign up for credit cards.

At an industry conference last month, Robert Isom, CEO of American, said the airline was expanding its loyalty programme at record rates. “A lot of that is driven by the free Wi-Fi,” he said.

Executives have also said that they are switching to Starlink because the earlier Internet services they offered were subpar. Executives at Alaska Airlines earlier this year said customer satisfaction was about 20 per cent higher on flights with Starlink.

But some industry experts say that most travellers pick airlines for many reasons, and Wi-Fi is not the most important one.

“People who are going to fly a lot in the future are going to self-select and gradually find the right programme that fits best for them,” said Jay Sorensen, who runs IdeaWorksCompany, an aviation industry consulting firm. “You can’t really create that.”

That doesn’t mean Wi-Fi is irrelevant. Like soft drinks and snacks, Internet access has become an expectation among passengers, Sorensen said.

Why is Musk feuding with Delta?

Most major US airlines upgrading to high-speed Wi-Fi are going with Starlink, whose satellites orbit closer to Earth than older satellites.

American, Alaska, United and Southwest Airlines have selected Starlink. But Delta, the most profitable US airline, and JetBlue have chosen Amazon Leo, a satellite service that is not yet available.

After Delta announced the partnership this year, Musk said the airline “wanted to make it painful, difficult and expensive for their customers”.

Then, he said Delta’s CEO Ed Bastian had made an error that could cost him his position. Musk was responding to an unverified report that Bastian had said it was not wise to work with Musk.

In an interview with The New York Times, Bastian disputed that report.

“I wouldn’t say that in a public setting or a private setting,” he said. “What we said is that we’re not working with Starlink because we decided to go a different direction.”

On Friday, Delta reported US$20.2 billion in revenue for the three months ended Sep 30, a company record.

SpaceX and Amazon did not respond to requests for comment.

This isn’t the first time Musk has criticised executives, politicians and others he disagrees with. In addition to Bastian, his targets have included Jeff Bezos, executive chair of Amazon, and Ryanair CEO Michael O’Leary.

Delta’s decision to use Leo could be risky. While other airlines have already begun offering Starlink service on some flights, Delta will not begin installing Amazon’s service until 2028.

That doesn’t mean Delta is not making upgrades, Bastian said. One of the airline’s current Internet providers, Viasat, recently launched two new satellites that will “change the game for our customers”, he said.

Bastian has said that Delta chose Amazon because it will cost the airline less than Starlink, and because the airline hopes to provide customers other perks from Amazon.

Delta has been profitable in recent years partly because customers like its credit cards, lounges and partnerships with other companies. For example, Delta’s customers can earn miles by buying coffee at Starbucks and hailing rides on Uber.

“We’ll be working very closely with them to bring new experiences to customers,” he said of Amazon. “It’s not just about the Wi-Fi; it’s what you do with the Wi-Fi.” NYTIMES

data.title: India built the worldâs largest digital payments system for free. Now, it must protect it
data.description:
[NEW DELHI] India’s success stories are often embroiled in controversies given the country’s divisive political climate. If government supporters are keen to tout them, critics are equally quick to question them.

But there is one success story that has risen above these divisions – the country’s instant real-time digital payments system, or Unified Payments Interface (UPI).

Regardless of one’s political leanings, there is no disputing that UPI has transformed the way Indians pay for goods.

Whether it’s jewellery or jalebis, pants or pakodas, paying for goods no longer involves handling grubby old currency notes.

Instead, a quick scan of the retailer’s QR code and a few taps on your smartphone app are all it takes. No fuss over figuring out how to return the exact change either.

The ease has proved addictive.

From just 373 transactions in its first month after it was introduced in April 2016, the system has grown to over 24 billion transactions in September 2026. That is more than 27,700 transactions in just the time it takes you to read this sentence.

What is even better is that the payments system has been free for users, both customers and merchants.

But soon this will no longer be the case, with the authorities having paved the way for fees to keep UPI running, a decision that has thrown the payments system into the thick of a raging debate.

Starting on Oct 15, merchants will have to pay a charge of 0.4 per cent for every transaction over 2,000 rupees (about S$27).

This merchant discount rate (MDR) has been capped at 300 rupees for transactions of 75,000 rupees or more.

Payments of more than 2,000 rupees for certain key services such as at petrol pumps and railways, on the other hand, involve a flat fee of five rupees.

Customers, however, remain unaffected, and every person-to-person transfer, regardless of the amount, will also be free.

Small merchants – those with UPI QR-code receipts of less than 100,000 rupees per month – will also continue to enjoy a mandatory zero-MDR rate.

What’s the fear?

The move has generated anger among merchants, many of whom operate in a low-margin business environment.

This has prompted worries that they may pass on the cost to customers, thereby slowing UPI’s expansion in India and undermining the growth of a globally acknowledged exemplar of digital payments that has helped formalise large segments of India’s informal cash economy.

With about 554.9 million users on UPI, the system still has room left to grow in a country of more than 1.4 billion people.

Any additional charge, including an indirect cost imposed on customers, risks pushing people back to cash, especially in India’s price-sensitive markets.

At the heart of this debate are merchants such as Akhilesh Kumar, the 38-year-old owner of a shoe shop in Delhi’s Sarojini Nagar market, who was waiting for customers one afternoon in September.

Footfall has been low, he says, since the start of the war with Iran.

“Business is already down, and now this extra fee will only deepen my losses,” Kumar laments.

A back-of-the-envelope calculation puts the additional cost to his business because of the new MDR at around 2,000 rupees per month.

This, he says, will be difficult to cough up because of existing expenses such as wages for his staff and taxes, as well as charges he must pay card companies, among other costs.

MDRs for card payments range from 1.5 to 2.5 per cent in India, which often prompts merchants to illegally demand an extra charge from customers or ask for payment in cash.

Kumar, however, acknowledges that if he tries demanding extra payment from customers for using UPI – which accounts for seven out of every 10 transactions at his store – they will simply go to another shop.

“I will have to pay for this charge out of my pocket, what else?” he says, demanding that the authorities take steps to revoke the MDR on UPI payments.

Why pay?

Even though UPI has been free for its users, maintaining its infrastructure involves costs.

According to one estimate, it costs as much as 207 billion rupees each year to keep the system running, including expenses on infrastructure maintenance, server capacity, cybersecurity and banking networks.

Even in Brazil, where the retail digital instant payments system known as Pix is celebrated widely, businesses pay an average fee of 0.22 per cent per transaction.

According to the National Payments Corporation of India, an umbrella organisation owned and operated by public and private banks that oversees the UPI system, the funds generated from the MDR will be used to enhance the efficiency of digital payments, as well as extend financial assistance to ecosystem players for merchant onboarding and incentivising the growth of the system.

Players here include the Walmart-backed PhonePe and Alphabet’s Google Pay, two platforms that together account for nearly 80 per cent of the country’s UPI transactions.

Without a way to charge users for their services, not only do players have little incentive to innovate, but even basic services can suffer at times.

UPI has suffered from rare but recurring outages in recent years, increasing scrutiny of the system’s infrastructure and its ability to scale reliably.

The longest such outage, lasting about 300 minutes, was in April 2025.

“Without people getting incentives or rewards for maintaining the system, this was only going to happen more and more,” says Anupam Manur, who teaches economics at the Takshashila Institution in Bengaluru.

He expects the new fee – which analysts project could generate about 200 billion rupees annually – to ensure UPI’s long-term reliability and sustainability, besides boosting innovation with products such as micro-credit loans on the platform.

But is it fair to get UPI users to pay when the system is already generating significant savings, possibly much more than what it takes to keep UPI running?

These savings include the reduced need to print currency notes and, as Ram Sewak Sharma, a retired Indian civil servant and former chairman of the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India, tells me, savings that banks accumulate from reductions in the costs of over-the-counter transactions or ATMs used to dispense currency notes.

Then there are bank earnings from additional funds that remain within the formal banking system as individuals keep money in their accounts to use on UPI rather than let it sit idle in their pockets as cash.

In fact, Sharma argues that savings from UPI are far higher than what it takes to keep the system running each year, so much so that he even thinks it is the government and banks that should be paying to run UPI, not merchants or individual users.

“Why should the consumers be charged for something that is not costing anything and which is benefiting the ecosystem so much?” he asks.

“My fear,” Sharma adds, “is that ultimately, people will end up paying and banks will end up enriching themselves.”

A situation where banks and corporates benefit more from UPI than individuals would be antithetical to the raison d’etre of UPI, which was built as public digital infrastructure with substantial government support.

Over the years, UPI has had an outsized influence, not only formalising large segments of India’s informal cash economy and ensuring better tax compliance, but also boosting the growth of small businesses and allowing people to transfer money with ease.

“There are multiple benefits (from the usage of UPI), and therefore I think the government must preserve those benefits and actually promote them rather than putting a charge, which is quite unjustified,” notes Sharma.

Proceed with caution

Irrespective of who pays for UPI’s upkeep, one thing is certain – the payments system is far too critical for stakeholders to botch it up.

This means they must track the impact of these charges on the system to ensure that they are put to good use and UPI continues to flourish.

A key thing to watch out for is whether the metrics around familiar UPI bugbears – such as outages, transaction decline rates and long dispute resolution times – improve.

“You have to demand accountability along with the money that they’re going to get,” says Takshashila Institution’s Manur, noting that banks and other stakeholders must make all relevant data publicly accessible.

And, if evidence shows that transaction growth has begun slowing down or perhaps even declining because of the new charges, the authorities should reconsider the MDR.

“Nobody should be dogmatic about this,” adds Manur, suggesting a lower flat fee if needed.

However, he cautions against making UPI free again, as it would be “the death knell of UPI, because no new innovation will happen”.

Another concern is the dominance of big players in the UPI ecosystem, which could end up hurting consumer interests in the long run.

“New fintech companies should be able to enter and compete without excessive regulatory burden while also having the flexibility to recover service costs from consumers,” notes Shrey Madaan, India country associate for Consumer Choice Center, a Washington-based non-profit organisation.

Moreover, the government has to be more sincere and honest in its communications about UPI, which it has not been.

In June 2025, it said that “speculation and claims that the MDR will be charged on UPI transactions are completely false, baseless, and misleading”, only to introduce it just a little more than a year later.

Users fear that current exemptions could be done away with next, or additional charges introduced.

There are also concerns around claims that the fee has been introduced to address US grievances, as UPI has eaten into the market share of Visa and Mastercard in India, an allegation the government has denied.

For now, the MDR charges look set to kick in on Oct 15 despite sporadic protests and viral photos of posters showing merchants discouraging UPI payments.

The authorities must ensure that UPI, something all Indians are genuinely proud of, continues to thrive and does not become a victim of its success. THE STRAITS TIMES

data.title: Inside Singaporeâs government team that kills its own products
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] If Li Hongyi had his way, he would run the public sector quite differently.

In some ways, he already does. Open Government Products (OGP), the experimental team he founded in 2019 to develop tech-enabled solutions for citizens and the public sector, operates more like a tech company than a government unit. It publishes detailed report cards on the products it has built, including their usage, quarterly costs, and the number of employees supporting them. This practice offers a level of disclosure that is uncommon even among private companies.

To date, OGP has developed over 40 products, including the ParkingSG app and RedeemSG, the digital voucher system used by millions of Singaporeans. Building tech products within the public sector can be a slow process. Some of the unit’s products take months to find their first user. Getting around red tape requires persistence – and sometimes ingenuity.

A few moments before our interview, Li took the stage at Tech in Asia Conference 2026 to share how almost every single one of OGP’s products exploits a “bureaucratic vulnerability” in some way. This lets them get shipped faster: ParkingSG, for instance, does not require a username or password. Personal data is stored on a user’s device rather than the application, reducing the government’s security burden.

Still, many of the team’s offerings face resistance. In 2024, an OGP-developed product drew complaints after many users reported difficulties using the web-based booking platform for public sports facilities such as badminton courts.

Yet a career in technology was not always what Li had in mind.

He may be the son of Lee Hsien Loong, Singapore’s former prime minister, but all he wanted to do as a child was “play and make video games”. Li also excelled in school, which eventually earned him a government scholarship to attend the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. The plan was to pursue physics and economics. He had largely accepted that his path would be linear: studying, getting good grades, and returning to a government ministry to “write some policies”.

A Google internship changed the course, however. Later, he swapped physics for computer science.

Li speaks fast, words and ideas spilling out. He is verbose, charismatic, and very convincing – an important trait to have when your job is, in a nutshell, to convince people there are better ways to be doing things. In this interview, Li explains how OGP gets things built inside a bureaucracy, what the public sector can learn from high-performing private companies, and why he believes culture cannot simply be built.

This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.

Every January, OGP does a monthlong hackathon where employees identify problems to build solutions for. What is the cost of doing this and why is it worthwhile? It is everyone’s work for a month, which is very substantial for an organization of our size. The question is: How much more information does it give you?

There are different kinds of games you play. There are games where all the information is available, in which case, if you plan and think hard enough, you can find the right solution. There are also games where information is hidden, and so you need to pay for information.

That same thing is true in innovation. If you acknowledge upfront that you are working in an ambiguous space, is (spending) one month out of a year – which is maybe 7 per cent of your annual productivity – to get information valuable? Yes.

When there is not enough budget, especially, we should invest a little bit of time and resources exploring ideas so that the remaining 93 per cent of our effort is spent on the right things, versus just randomly.

A few months ago, your engineering team did an AMA (Ask Me Anything) on Reddit where it answered questions – candidly – about how it builds and prioritises ideas. How did that idea come about, and was it from you?

Absolutely not my idea. I was actually on leave at the time.

The reason why I called the team Open Government Products is that I wanted the word “open” in it. I wanted a word that would tell people we work differently, and I think “open” is not how people generally describe the government, although it is a very important part of a modern, well-functioning team and community.

In fact, if you look at high-performing teams, you will notice everyone says you must have open communication: You must be honest about what you are doing. You must have clarity and visibility. You must be accountable to the public.

And so, at OGP, I try very hard to push for an open culture where people talk and disagree openly so that we can have the right information and solve problems.

From the marketing team’s perspective, we are trying to get people to join us, and we are trying to push forward that open culture. I think it is a great idea.

I try to run the team in a way that I am not ashamed of anything we do. You can tell anyone anything about how we choose our products, how we run our performance, how we make critical decisions, and I will be happy to defend it.

The mistake a lot of government agencies make when engaging with the public is being overly defensive about how people will try to hurt them.

You were a product manager at Google. What is the biggest difference between building products for the private sector versus the public sector?

When I was working at Google, for something as simple as the shade of blue you use for ads, you would have a data scientist, a product manager, and some engineers running an experiment for a couple of weeks. You could find that a particular shade gets you a 2 per cent increase in clicks, which seems like nothing, but at Google scale, that is billions of dollars. It is tremendous.

If you were to tell your friends and family what you did today, that you made the color of ads 2 per cent lighter or something and therefore increased revenue – who cares?

In the government, you would be creating something like a subsidy scheme for single mothers or figuring out how to help social workers plan their tools. It is super important, but you do not have the data – you do not have the ability to run experiments. You are just talking to various people, getting a feel in the dark, and then moving.

At Google, you are solving really small problems with the best tools and the best resources in the world. In the government, you are solving massive problems, and you feel like you are just fighting with sticks and rocks. To me, that was the big mental shift.

Was that experience at Google what convinced you there was a different way to build things?

The key thing for me at Google was that it gave me a view of a different way of doing things. There are other ways of doing things that work just as well, and the Singaporean way is not the only way.

It is like trying to convince you that giraffes do not exist. For a long time, people thought giraffes were mythical. But having seen a giraffe, nothing in the world can convince you a giraffe does not exist.

I feel the same way about organisational design.

When you’re in Singapore, everyone will try to convince you that no, it is impossible: You cannot do this very liberal, open-communication thing. You cannot do this experimental thing.

But good organisations with modern design, open culture, and mission-driven people do exist. I have seen them.

I think the difference between Google employees or MIT students and Singapore students is that they are willing to try things, experiment, explore, and build things.

You’ve brought some of that experimentation into OGP, which operates somewhat differently from other parts of the government. Does the team have fewer constraints than other government agencies?

One of the misconceptions people have about OGP is that we operate with fewer constraints. Actually, at some level, we operate with a much bigger constraint: If we do not deliver, we do not exist.

The deal I made for OGP was like a venture capital (VC) deal. It is like saying, “look, don’t bother me with all of these procurement and compliance and sort of procedural things. Instead, every year, I’ll put together a presentation and a report to the bosses on what we spent and what we accomplished. If you like it, you can give me more (funding)”.

We started with 20 people, and I remember the first year we reported that we had done good work, and so we had 40 people the next year.

But at any point – and we have done this – if we do not deliver our outcomes, and the bosses decide to give us less funding, I will have to let people go. I think that is, to me, both scary and the right (level of) accountability.

In fact, for Halloween two years ago, our theme was “dead products”, and we put up little pins across the office for all the products we killed. We have to force efficiency so people on those products can be reallocated to products that are more promising.

OGP now employs just under 250 people. As the unit grows, how do you preserve that way of working without becoming more bureaucratic? Is there a critical size at which OGP’s bottom-up culture starts to break down?

I do not think culture is a goal. Culture is the outcome of being clear about what you want to do.

Everyone wants a good culture, but you cannot steer culture directly. What you can set are the goals, systems, accountability, incentives – and culture emerges from that.

You need to understand what lets you work well as a small organisation and make sure you enable that.

I am not trying to take the team that was successful at 50 people and make it a 500-person team. I am trying to look at what that team did and ask what I can do to have 10 of that.

Now that we have like four or five 50-person teams, I am shifting to a completely different job, where I’m running an incubator or a VC. My job is to support people doing what I was doing, even if I cannot do it myself.

Surely not all experiments work. OGP spent S$4.4 million (US$3.4 million) developing an alternative to Singapore’s electronic road pricing system (ERP) over two years, but it wasn’t ultimately rolled out. How do you decide whether an experiment like that was still worthwhile?

Therein lies the core challenge of public service. You cannot just use profit for any of these measures.

As a country, and given that the scale of ERP 2.0 is S$500 million, how much should we be spending to explore an alternative?

S$100 million is probably too much. S$50 million is still quite high. But if you say 1 per cent (of that), I think that is reasonable.

Our experiment cost over S$4 million. Maybe it does not come into play now, but in five or 10 years, you are going to have to do a replacement for ERP 2.0 again.

You are going to need to understand what your options are. You are going to need this information, and you (should) pay 1 per cent for much better information.

If we took 1 per cent of the cost of all major government infrastructure projects and allocated it to exploring alternatives, which might be better in the future, I think as a nation we would be better off, and that is the kind of calculus you have to make.

We work with the Land Transport Authority quite a lot on this, and it now understands how all these systems work. It can now use that to plan what its future objectives are.

You’ve spent years trying to build products within the government. Has that given you a different view of where the public sector still falls short – and where tech can make the biggest difference?

If what my bosses tell me is true, I have a very poor understanding of how the government operates.

I have seen what companies do to help you search the internet, watch videos, and buy shampoo – and their processes are way better than what we are doing to help people get access to healthcare and help underprivileged people get educated.

At Google, we had an internal website where you could watch videos of all the cafeterias via webcams so that you did not have to waste time walking there to get food if it was crowded. Whereas the process of helping people who cannot afford private healthcare access healthcare is ineffective. That, to me, is unconscionable.

I think the core problem with the world is that all the smartest people are working on the dumbest problems.

If you want to sell shampoo, you have got teams of PhD holders figuring this out, down to the wording and the size of the thumbnail. If you want to do a filter, you have got tons of computer vision experts, the best people in the world, getting paid hundreds of thousands of dollars a year to make it.

But if you are trying to, for example, (create a solution) so social workers (can) keep track of what (their) clients are and share data about, like, what kind of assistance they need, we are doing things on paper. We are texting each other back and forth.

I remember we were talking to some of the people who were arranging transport for children in foster care. Grab, for your bubble tea, has this sophisticated logistics system. But for children who are in foster care and need to go back and forth from schools with proper chaperones all along the way, arrangements are made on WhatsApp groups.

It is hundreds of these little WhatsApp groups texting each other and hoping that you coordinate and nothing falls through the cracks. I think that is wrong, and that is why I feel this is worth doing.

If that gap is what motivates OGP’s work, what kind of person do you look for to work on these problems?

The phrase I use when I describe the ideal OGP employee is someone who is angsty but hopeful.

If you are just pessimistic, you are useless to me because everything sucks, and nothing can be done. If you are just optimistic, you are also useless to me because if everything is very good, then you have no reason to try and fix things.

You need to see both: where the world is and where it could be, as well as the gap in between. And that gap is the tension that pulls you to do things. TECH IN ASIA

data.title: What real mental health support at work can look like
data.description:
WORLD Mental Health Day falls on Saturday (Oct 10). This year’s theme is “Lived Experiences Heard: Real Voices, Real Change”, which emphasises the importance of listening to people and urging changes in policy and the workplace.

Despite increased awareness of mental health in Singapore, a critical question remains: Have we achieved pervasive, actual implementation of real and tangible support for people with mental health conditions in our workplaces?

The honest answer is no.

Stigma continues to be real and present. Many who live with – or suspect they have – a mental health condition do not dare to voice what they are experiencing.

And many still do not seek help, fearing backlash, unspoken bias or being quietly sidelined in the office.

Surprisingly, or perhaps not, this hesitation is deeply ingrained in our work culture. It was evident even within my organisation, the Singapore Association for Mental Health.

In a closed-door consultation I held with colleagues shortly after stepping into the role of CEO, most indicated they were unsure whether to share that they have a condition.

Some were afraid of the potential repercussions of being seen simply attending a session on mental health with the CEO, wondering whether confidentiality would truly be kept.

This took place even though I had openly shared my personal lived experience at a staff town hall just months prior.

The takeaway was sobering. If employees inside an agency devoted entirely to psychiatric recovery still wrestle with the vulnerability of being seen having mental health conditions, the silence inside our wider commercial workplaces must undoubtedly be profound.

Rather than dictating policy from behind a closed boardroom door, we used our workplace to figure out what real, practical support looks like on the ground. I sent an open note inviting staff to sit down with me to co-develop these guidelines together.

At the first discussion, only a handful stepped forward. There was genuine apprehension in the room. Before we could even talk about policy, my priority was simply allaying fear, reassuring colleagues that it was safe to be present and their perspectives were essential.

I shared some thoughts on flexible work arrangements, and heard their questions and concerns first-hand.

By the second meeting, word had travelled that it was a safe space, and that leadership genuinely wanted a mental health framework co-developed. We had new joiners at the meetings.

This time, the discussions went straight into the real, thorny issues: How do we evaluate performance fairly? How do we prevent supervisor bias during appraisals? What practical handles do middle managers need so they do not panic, overstep or judge?

We have our third session coming up soon. For us, pace is the focus, not speed. Giving staff the space and time to reflect and align is key.

Facilitated co-development, coupled with genuine team ownership, will ultimately make internal policies, especially those related to sensitive and personal matters, work.

Three operational changes

The Workplace Fairness Act, which will protect employees from being discriminated against based on mental health conditions, is set to be enforced in 2027. With this, corporate Singapore can no longer rely on superficial wellness perks or passive hotlines to signal support.

Grounded in what we have learned from our own internal journey, we propose that companies need to move from intent to action in three distinct operational levels.

First, there must be genuine buy-in at the leadership level. Company leaders need to see that a compassionate culture is not a soft human-resources exercise, but a standard staff-retention and sustained-performance strategy.

Top-level backing is necessary to establish clear procedural protection, such as a confidential safe-disclosure pathway in which an employee can request temporary adjustments, with the assurance that performance will be judged on output rather than face time, and that their career mobility will not be jeopardised.

Second, HR professionals need to establish structured, phased return-to-work protocols.

Consider a simple reality check: If an employee breaks a leg, they go to a doctor, take medical leave and return to daily activity gradually, as the leg heals. You would never expect them to run a marathon on their first day back at work.

A severe mental health condition warrants the exact same operational logic. Expecting someone recovering from clinical depression or severe burnout to jump straight back into an intense 45-hour workweek invites immediate relapse.

A practical return-to-work framework means maintaining light-touch contact during medical leave to agree on what colleagues are told regarding health accommodations, returning to work with reduced hours or lighter duties, and holding regular review check-ins to calibrate workloads before ramping up to, and resuming, full responsibilities.

Lastly, front-line supervisors and managers must be equipped with practical handles. This, I believe, will be the toughest part for most organisations.

Managers do not need to become counsellors or clinicians. Expecting them to diagnose or provide therapy is unrealistic and counterproductive.

What they need is the training and confidence to put across that performance remains the key assessment metric, while maintaining empathy and fairness in their reviews.

That means learning to spot early behavioural shifts, asking constructive workload-focused check-in questions and having clear referral boundaries, so they can connect struggling staff to professional support without awkwardness or fear.

Ultimately, moving from policy to practice will transform workplace well-being. Side effects from medication and the day-to-day realities of our conditions do not make us any less responsible; they are standard challenges along a recovery curve.

We all want to engage in meaningful, dignified work and be contributing members of the team.

When employees know their employer offers tangible structures to navigate human vulnerability, they are motivated to give their best. Slowly, stigma will be reduced, and hopefully, eliminated.

The writer is CEO of the Singapore Association for Mental Health

data.title: Trump says Putin to supply US with diesel ahead of November midterms
data.description:
[WASHINGTON] US President Donald Trump is working with Vladimir Putin to release Russian diesel supplies into global markets, a move that upends years of sanctions as the White House seeks ways to tame soaring fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections.

Trump announced on Friday (Oct 9) a series of cargoes beginning this month totalling about 13.5 million barrels, initially.

The Kremlin published a statement citing Putin, who said Russia was ready “to supply oil and petroleum products to the US and global markets”.

The US Treasury also issued a waiver for previously sanctioned Russian fuel.

“That is massive amounts of oil coming into our country, and I want to thank President Putin,” Trump said to reporters at the White House on Friday. “And it’s diesel, which is what we want”.

Diesel, the fuel often dubbed the workhorse of the global economy, has been thrust into the spotlight as a massive supply crunch sent pump prices to records and stoked concerns over energy-driven inflation.

Ahead of US midterms in November, the Trump administration is making a series of moves aimed at bringing down prices, which have raised costs for farmers and truckers.

But the Russia action risks sparking geopolitical backlash without boosting supply enough to lower prices significantly.

US diesel futures fell on the news to trade at about US$4.66 a gallon, still at seasonal all-time highs.

Since July, Russia has operated under a self-imposed diesel export ban following months of punishing attacks on its refineries from Ukrainian drones.

Those attacks have continued through recent days, but Russia is beginning to lift its restrictions on diesel exports immediately, ahead of schedule, Tass reported, citing Alexander Novak, the nation’s deputy prime minister responsible for energy.

Move has drawn criticism

The Trump-Putin agreement has drawn the ire of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Russian attacks on Ukraine have killed dozens in just recent days, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a post on X earlier Friday.

Kyiv has been facing blackouts, with hospitals and schools among Russian targets.

“Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world,” Zelenskyy said in a post on X.

“Russia will ‘repay’ the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged.”

US Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer also criticised the move.

“Trump is doing a deal with the devil to try to help his flailing political fortunes from the shockingly high diesel prices,” Schumer said in a post on X.

While Trump has previously called upon Ukraine to halt its attacks on Russian oil infrastructure, the country has instead intensified its strikes on Russian oil assets in a bid to curb the Kremlin’s ability to finance and sustain its war.

“Ukraine will not set Russian oil refineries on fire if Russia does not destroy our energy infrastructure. This is the kind of agreement we are proposing to America, and we believe the United States has enough power to achieve such a compromise,” Zelenskyy said.

Trump was read Zelenskyy’s comments by a reporter at the White House, and the US leader responded: “We are a strong partner.”

“We need oil for the world, and this is diesel, which is what we need. So we’re very happy to get it,” Trump said.

Trump announced a set of initial product releases beginning with 2.25 million barrels in October, 3.75 million in November and 7.5 million “immediately thereafter”.

Novak confirmed Russia is ready to supply that amount of fuel, with the 7.5 million barrels released in December.

Trump added that “based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel” – equal to about 22.5 million barrels.

There are concerns over whether Russian energy infrastructure is in strong enough condition to meet those goals, said Ryan McKay, senior commodity strategist at TD Securities.

“The biggest concern is the refiners being able to do it,” McKay said.

But even if the promised barrels are released, the impact would be marginal, McKay said.

That is particularly true of the most immediate October release of just 2.5 million barrels – around 10 per cent of the barrels Russia exported per month before Ukraine’s campaign intensified.

“Those barrels could help, but they may not fully materialise, and what does arrive could still be too little, too late,” said Rebecca Babin, senior energy trader at CIBC Private Wealth Group.

“The headline may move prices initially, but this is hardly a straightforward solution.”

US retail diesel prices stood at US$6.28 a gallon as at Thursday, below record highs above US$6.50 set in September.

Zelenskyy has tried to keep Trump on his side as Russia has maintained round-the-clock assaults on Ukrainian civil infrastructure.

Ukrainian negotiators were set to meet US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in the US on Friday.

Trump on Friday claimed the releases of Russian supply would help lower diesel prices for American farmers, ranchers and truckers – key voting blocs ahead of November midterm elections in which costs of living, including for energy, are the dominant issue.

Polls show Trump at record-low approval ratings and voters largely disappointed in his handling of the economy and war in Iran.

The prolonged conflict has crunched energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz, raising fuel prices globally.

Trump said earlier this week that he would not strike Iran again until after the November midterms, indicating what he said were productive discussions with Teheran.

Meanwhile, other global restrictions remain in place on Russian fuel supplies.

Before Ukraine’s attacks accelerated this spring, the bulk of seaborne Russian exports went to Europe outside the European Union, Africa, Asia and Brazil.

The US last imported diesel from Russia in March 2022, according to Energy Information Administration data.

Trump on Friday did not indicate if he discussed any other topics with Putin, such as the recent death of a laboratory worker in Siberia that prompted speculation about pneumonic plague, or about recent US efforts to jump-start peace talks to end the Kremlin’s war in Ukraine. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Issue 215: Coalâs role in South-east Asian energy security; Singaporeâs electricity import woes
data.description:
Energy transition

Beware the overly narrow view of energy security

The reframing of the renewable energy transition as a matter of security instead of a climate priority has been a mixed bag for climate action.

On one hand, the security impetus has fuelled a desire among many countries to diversify away from oil and gas towards more renewable sources of energy. However, the pursuit of energy security has also rekindled the lifespan for coal, especially in countries like Indonesia or Vietnam where domestic coal resources exist.

An important lesson lies beneath that dynamic: The energy transition cannot be tackled as a one-dimensional problem, or it will fall short. Just as the climate change movement has learnt that the energy transition cannot happen at the expense of energy resilience and security, the pursuit of secure energy must be undertaken with the understanding that global warming is ultimately destabilising. Coal and fossil fuel policies should not close a window but leave the door open.

That dissonance between the climate-first and security-first approaches in the energy transition is apparent in the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) Asean Energy Security Review, which projects that while renewables will capture a larger share of electricity generation in South-east Asia in the next five years, coal and gas generation will continue to grow as well.

The review’s projections trace from a fundamental expectation of growing energy needs in the region. For instance, electricity demand in South-east Asia is expected to grow at an average of 5.4 per cent every year from 2026 to 2030 on the back of growing demand for cooling, data centres and industry.

The security question as addressed by the review is how to “ensure the uninterrupted availability of energy at affordable prices, while maintaining the flexibility and resilience needed to manage shocks and longer-term stresses”.

The review’s recommendations are centred on three key strategies: Diversify energy supply sources and routes, make greater use of domestically available energy resources, and accelerate electrification alongside efficiency improvements.

Renewables tick many boxes. For example, the review describes South-east Asia’s solar supply chain self-sufficiency as “among the world’s most secure” with existing manufacturing capacity able to supply projected regional demand across solar modules, cells and wafers.

Looking ahead, the review expects wind generation in South-east Asia to grow by about 26 per cent annually from 2026 to 2030, while solar generation could grow by about 23 per cent a year over the same period. Together, solar and wind’s share of the region’s electricity mix will increase to 11 per cent by 2030 from about 5 per cent in 2025.

The security challenge for greater adoption of renewables in the region has less to do with generation capacity and more with improving grid and storage infrastructure to handle the inherent variability of solar and wind generation.

But renewables are not the only source of energy that is growing. The review projects that coal demand in the region will grow by about 4.4 per cent annually through 2030, the fastest pace globally. Indonesia, the world’s largest coal exporter, accounts for more than 56 per cent of the growth, with Vietnam and the Philippines also growing coal generation in the coming years.

The reason is simple: Self-reliance is the key to energy security. If you’re a coal-producing country like Indonesia or Vietnam, the logical thing to do for energy security is to continue to use coal.

Coal is also a cheap and energy-dense fuel. The widespread use of captive coal plants – off-grid coal generators – for industrial uses in Indonesia also makes coal difficult to replace without significant costs to communities and economies.

“Indonesia has committed to reach net zero by 2060 or earlier,” the review notes. “This presents some challenges as coal is expected to remain important for both the power and industrial sectors, particularly for nickel processing. Coal is also an important provider of jobs, as well as state revenues through taxes and royalties. Some regions in Indonesia, such as East and South Kalimantan, are among the most coal-dependent regions in the world.”

Nevertheless, the review highlights the risks of continued dependence on coal without plans to transition to greener alternatives.

For example, continued reliance on captive coal in nickel production “may raise future transition costs, complicate net zero pathways and create export risks if importing Asean member states apply stricter sustainability standards to nickel supply chains”.

There is a danger in taking too narrow a view when framing the energy transition as a security issue.

There is no doubt that sufficient and reliable energy is essential for countries, especially in fast-growing South-east Asia. But policymakers and businesses must take a more holistic approach to energy security.

First, policies need to consider long-term security alongside short-term needs. Coal and natural gas may keep the lights on for now, but are these solutions that would still make sense a few decades from now?

Second, climate change needs to be recognised as a security concern as well. The planet-scale impact of climate change – weather catastrophes and agricultural losses, for instance – has the potential to cause tremendous disruptions to social and economic systems. Lights at night are important, but so is food at mealtimes. The impact is also widespread across many vectors – for example, higher temperatures can reduce the efficiency of solar panels.

The shift in the energy transition conversation to one dominated by energy security has helped to highlight the benefits of renewable energy beyond being greener. But it is important to ensure that the new paradigm does not devolve into short-sighted actions concerned only with geopolitics. Just because a war in the Middle East is highly consequential at the moment does not mean that climate change has lessened or that climate needs are no longer pressing.

Energy transition

Time to sharpen Singapore’s energy transition strategy

It seems increasingly likely that Singapore will miss its interim climate goals as a major energy import strategy struggles to progress quickly enough.

Singapore is likely to miss its target of importing about 6 gigawatts (GW) of low-carbon electricity by 2035, says research firm Wood Mackenzie. As a result, green electricity imports will probably account for only about 15 per cent of the electricity mix by 2035, about half of the targeted one-third contribution.

Wood Mackenzie’s projection is based on the fact that although Singapore has approved 9.25 GW of import projects, none of that capacity has begun construction. The analysis identifies a few key hurdles that hold back progress: “Export permit frameworks, project bankability, cross-border transmission financing, and the lack of a complete market mechanism that allows Singapore buyers to claim the carbon value of imported electricity.”

The challenge for Singapore is that none of these hurdles are fully within its control. For example, Wood Mackenzie notes that Vietnam still has no legal mechanism for a foreign developer to develop generation and to export it through a dedicated undersea cable. Cambodia lacks an export regulatory framework and surplus generation, with blackouts a regular occurrence. The firm does not expect exports from either country by 2035.

Singapore has pledged, under the terms of the Paris climate agreement, to reduce greenhouse gas emissions to 60 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (MtCO2e) by 2030 after peaking earlier. By 2035, the country aims to reduce emissions further to between 45 and 50 MtCO2e.

Singapore’s emissions remain on an upward trajectory. Singapore reported national emissions of 55.5 MtCO2e for 2023. The country’s total electricity generation in 2023 was 57.4 terawatt hours (TWh). In 2025, generation increased about 5 per cent to 60.4 TWh. Singapore’s grid emissions factor declined only about half of that between 2023 and 2024.

Electricity demand is also growing faster than initially expected. In a September call for bids to develop additional gas-fired generation by 2031 and 2032, the Energy Market Authority revised its earlier outlook for peak demand. The official projection is now for peak demand to increase at a compound annual growth rate of 2.9 to 6.5 per cent from 2025 to 2034, higher than the initial forecast of 2.4 to 4.8 per cent.

Singapore will probably have to revise its climate targets to better align them with current circumstances, but the more important task is to review the climate strategy to find ways to hasten progress on the country’s energy transition.

Energy imports seem unavoidable for resource-starved Singapore, so Singapore needs to sharpen its plan to overcome the hurdles to progress. Those hurdles were not all apparent when Singapore’s Energy 2050 Committee first formalised imports as a key pillar of the energy transition in 2022, but now they are. Reviewing the climate goals present an opportunity to be more focused about addressing these roadblocks.

The green-alternatives pillar can also be better focused on pathways that are more promising. Green hydrogen may not be as likely as once thought with viable scale still elusive. Nuclear looks increasingly like the most feasible way to lower domestic generation emissions. The geothermal pathway is still very nascent, but it could be worth accelerating research so that its feasibility can be determined sooner.

data.title: Singapore stands ready to assist Indonesia amid worsening haze, Grace Fu in touch with counterpart
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Singapore stands ready to assist Indonesia amid the worsening haze conditions and forest fires, said Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (MSE) Grace Fu, who is in touch with her Indonesian counterpart.

“We are in touch with our neighbours. As you know, this is an area where, because of El Nino, we are facing very dry weather in the region, and therefore it has made forest fires a lot harder to put out,” Fu told the media at Our Tampines Hub on Saturday (Oct 10).

“We are aware that efforts are going on. We stand ready to assist where we can,” said Fu, adding that she has been in touch with Indonesia’s Minister of Environment Jumhur Hidayat to offer her support and express appreciation for his efforts to contain the forest fires.

Fu also said she supports any regional efforts to have discussions on regional cooperation on haze issues.

The 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) – a measure of air quality in Singapore – hit 192 in central Singapore at 6pm on Oct 9, the highest so far in 2026. It was inching towards very unhealthy levels of 201.

The air quality in Singapore improved marginally overnight but still remained within the unhealthy band in the morning of Saturday. At 9 am, the PSI readings were: north (124), south (135), east (156), west (160), and central (174).

The one-hour PM2.5 levels – which point to the current air quality and are used as a gauge for immediate activities – were also elevated in all five regions, ranging from values of 80 to 119.

While Singapore has been experiencing several haze episodes since Sep 4, the current period is the longest with unhealthy air and haze particles lingering in the air since Oct 5.

The haze is coming from forest and land fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan, largely due to the use of fire to clear land for agriculture.

Thick, toxic smoke from burning peat is a major source of the haze. Fuelled by the ongoing El Nino, dried-out peatlands can burn for weeks once they catch fire and are notoriously difficult to put out.

Fu noted that the haze conditions has worsened over the past week due to increased hotspots in Sumatra and Kalimantan, and also because “the wind conditions has been unfavorable to us”.

“Although we expect some rain over the weekend, we could expect the haze level to exceed 200, going into the very unhealthy range,” she added.

“So we have to be prepared. We are very concerned for our population, particularly those that are more vulnerable.”

In June 2026, Singapore and Indonesia inked an agreement on environmental cooperation, which includes cooperation on transboundary pollution.

“We have been discussing possible long-term initiatives to mitigate transboundary haze, including the exchange of more early warning information as well as how Singapore could support the Asean Coordinating Centre for Transboundary Haze Pollution Control that would be hosted in Indonesia,” MSE told The Straits Times.

The interim coordinating centre, hosted in Jakarta, is a hub where Asean nations share information, prepare for fires and organise assistance.

During the last severe haze in 2015, when the PSI reached hazardous levels of above 300 and forced schools to shut for a day, Singapore helped Indonesia with firefighting operations.

The authorities said on Friday that N95 masks will be distributed to individuals who may be more vulnerable to the effects of haze or who may have limited means of obtaining them when air quality hits “very unhealthy” levels.

Such levels are denoted by a PSI reading between 201 and 300.

Mask vending machines will also be made available at selected public transport hubs and social services offices.

Those eligible to collect N95 masks include the Pioneer Generation, Merdeka Generation, CHAS orange and blue card holders, and children aged between seven and 16.

When air quality breaches the “very unhealthy” threshold, air-conditioned rooms in community clubs, and selected Residents’ Committee and Residents’ Network Centres, will also be set up as haze shelters for the public to seek respite in.

All preschools will also be required to cease all outdoor activities and strenuous indoor activities.

Children with chronic heart and lung conditions will be exempted from all indoor physical activities.

When air quality is in the “very unhealthy” range, outdoor work for employees with chronic heart and lung conditions should be avoided.

Fu added that there are sectoral guidance in place according to the PSI levels for schools, preschools, workplaces and healthcare institutions.

“You can find guidance from the sector leads, such as MOE coming up with an advisory on the different approaches with different levels of PSI,” she added. THE STRAITS TIMES

data.title: Stocks to watch: SIA, CapitaLand Investment
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Oct 8):

SIA : Singapore Airlines and Air India will offer standalone code-share flights and “enhanced” frequent-flyer benefits, giving passengers “greater flexibility” in trip planning with 126 weekly flights, the two carriers announced on Wednesday. The expanded offerings cover flights between Singapore and eight Indian cities: Ahmedabad, Bengaluru, Chennai, Delhi, Hyderabad, Kochi, Kolkata and Mumbai. Shares of SIA ended at S$6.68 on Wednesday, S$0.02 or 0.3 per cent lower.

CapitaLand Investment : CapitaLand Investment and IOI Properties Group are now in exclusive due diligence for the acquisition of One Raffles Place, with a 50-50 joint bid submitted to owners OUE Reit and UOB, IOI Properties Group CEO Lee Yeow Seng told The Business Times on Wednesday. The offer was made about three months ago. Shares of CapitaLand Investment ended 1.6 per cent or S$0.04 higher at S$2.49 on Wednesday.

data.title: Oil prices settle higher as more production shut ahead of hurricane
data.description:
[HOUSTON] Oil prices settled higher on Friday (Oct 9) as Hurricane Isaias churned towards the northern Gulf of Mexico and oil companies shut more than 70 per cent of crude production in US waters.

Earlier in the session, crude prices were down as US President Donald Trump said talks with Iran to end the war in the Middle East had been “productive”.

Trump also teased an upcoming, undisclosed announcement on diesel and said he was considering suspending the federal petrol tax.

Brent crude futures settled at US$104.72, up 44 cents or 0.42 per cent.

US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures finished at US$91.85 a barrel, up US$0.36, or 0.39 per cent.

Plans by China, the world’s top oil importer, to resume refined fuel exports after a brief halt during its Golden Week holiday, also weighed on the market, Reuters reported citing sources.

On a weekly basis, Brent and WTI prices are set to rise.

Trump’s Iran pledge along with China’s resumption of product exports were moving prices lower, PVM Oil Associates analyst Tamas Varga said.

Prices have been volatile as threats to shipping in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, which carried shipments equal to about 20 per cent of global oil and fuel before the war, have increased.

Trump said Washington was having “productive discussions” with Iran and said no attack was planned before the Nov 3 midterm congressional elections after media reports that he was considering an attack before then.

Iran’s Tasnim news agency reported the same day that Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said Teheran is reviewing the US response to its proposal that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days.

The US is still pressuring Iran economically, imposing sanctions targeting individuals, networks and 17 vessels for transporting Iranian crude, oil products and petrochemicals.

The Iran war and the conflict between Russia and Ukraine have disrupted supplies of refined fuels such as petrol, jet fuel and especially diesel fuel.

The oil market is also contending with Hurricane Isaias in the Gulf of Mexico, where producers had shut in about 1.3 million barrels per day, or 62.9 per cent, of current oil production, according to the US Marine Minerals Administration. REUTERS
